title: Contacts to Low-Dimensional Semiconductors: Physical Theory and Analytical Model
abstract: Metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors are critical for nanoelectronics, yet a general physical description has remained elusive. We present an analytical model for metal-induced gap states (MIGS), revealing a universal scaling law governed by semiconductor dimensionality. Linking MIGS to transport observables, we provide a unified formulation of Schottky barrier height, transfer length, and contact resistance. Our model explains recent experiments on carbon nanotubes and 2D materials, clarifying the fundamental criteria for achieving scalable, low-resistance contacts.
summary: This work develops a unified analytical model describing metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors by focusing on Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS). It successfully links the fundamental physics of MIGS density, governed by semiconductor dimensionality, to measurable transport parameters like contact resistance and Schottky barrier height. The theory provides crucial diagnostic tools for engineering high-performance nanoelectronic devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a general physical theory for metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors, which dictates device performance in nanoelectronics.
main_result: The authors present an analytical model revealing universal scaling laws for Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS) and providing unified formulations for Schottky barrier height and contact resistance across different dimensions.
method: The theory uses Green's function formalism, Fermi's Golden Rule, and charge neutrality principles to derive expressions for MIGS density and transport properties.
model_or_system: The focus is on metal-semiconductor interfaces involving low-dimensional semiconductors (1D CNTs, 2D TMDs). The model explicitly incorporates the physics of Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS) which govern Fermi Level Pinning (FLP).
key_observables: Schottky barrier height ($\Phi_B$), contact resistance ($R_C$), transfer length ($L_t$), and MIGS density ($ho_X$).
important_parameters: Semiconductor dimensionality ($n$), coupling strength ($\Gamma(E)$), defect concentration (e.g., sulfur vacancies in $	ext{MoS}_2$), and metal work function ($E_{FM}$).
main_assumptions: The model relies on the effective-mass approximation for the semiconductor density of states and assumes that charge conservation principles can be mapped onto the Green's function formalism, though it extends beyond simple zero-crossing criteria.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dimensional dependence of conduction-band MIGS ($ho_c^X$) in 1D, 2D, and 3D, and show how $\Phi_B$ varies with CNT chirality or how $E_F$ de-pins when using semimetals.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the general physical problem (lack of theory) to deriving core equations for MIGS ($ho_X$), linking these states to macroscopic observables like $\Phi_B$ and $R_C$, and finally applying this framework to specific systems (CNTs, TMDs, semimetals).
why_interesting: While not directly related to quantum information protocols, the rigorous theoretical treatment of electronic structure at interfaces—a key area in open quantum systems—provides deep insights into how external coupling modifies intrinsic material properties.
